evidence.claim: Springs and steamboat towns along the St. Johns River corridor
evidence.quote: 1800s steamboat tourists utilized the St. Johns River

evidence.claim: The River of Lakes Heritage Corridor links St. Johns River communities and springs, with Sanford and DeLand as major anchors.
evidence.quote: including the larger anchors of DeLand and Sanford

evidence.claim: Multi-use trails often parallel the byway, and its spring stops include Blue, Gemini, Green and DeLeon springs.
evidence.quote: There are inviting multi-use trails, a part of the larger River-to-Sea Loop and Coast-to-Coast Trails, which often parallel the byway.

evidence.claim: its spring stops include Blue, Gemini, Green and DeLeon springs.
evidence.quote: This byway also features springs, including Blue Spring State Park, where manatees gather in winter, DeLeon Springs, with a famous pancake restaurant in the old Mill house, Gemini Springs, and Green Springs.

evidence.claim: Florida Scenic Highways describes the corridor through its history, contemporary culture and natural features.
evidence.quote: embodies a blend of history, sophisticated contemporary culture, and gorgeous natural Florida.

evidence.claim: The 156-mile corridor received state designation on March 12, 2009, followed by national designation in 2021.
evidence.quote: Byway Length: 156 Miles Designated: March 12, 2009, National Designation 2021

evidence.claim: Its communities had earlier depended on water transport: the DeLand area was originally accessible only by steamboat on the St. Johns.
evidence.quote: the area was originally accessible only by steamboat up the St. Johns River.

evidence.claim: At Blue Spring, Louis Thursby operated a landing by 1868, and nine steamboats eventually served it on regular routes, carrying freight, mail and travelers.
evidence.quote: By 1868 Thursby was running a steamboat landing on the river

evidence.claim: nine steamboats eventually served it on regular routes, carrying freight, mail and travelers.
evidence.quote: Nine steamboats eventually called there on regular routes, carrying freight, mail, tourists and sportsmen.

evidence.claim: A narrow-gauge railway connected Orange City with the landing in 1881, bringing citrus to the wharf.
evidence.quote: In 1881 a narrow-gauge railroad, the first in the county, was laid from Orange City to the landing.

evidence.claim: bringing citrus to the wharf.
evidence.quote: Mules hauled a wooden flatcar of citrus to a pasture on Thursby's land, and the car then rolled downhill to the wharf.

evidence.claim: That railway later became part of the Florida East Coast Railway in 1896; its paved-over bed is now Magnolia Avenue.
evidence.quote: became part of the Florida East Coast Railway in 1896. Its paved-over bed is now Magnolia Avenue.

evidence.claim: From Sanford, head toward DeBary and DeLand, with Blue Spring west of Orange City along the way.
evidence.quote: You can turn left to go to Sanford or you can turn right to head to Debary and DeLand.

evidence.claim: with Blue Spring west of Orange City along the way.
evidence.quote: Blue Spring State Park is a Florida state park located west of Orange City

evidence.claim: Continue through DeLand’s Woodland Boulevard historic district to DeLeon Springs, where the state park lies off County Road 3.
evidence.quote: It is located in DeLeon Springs, off CR 3.

evidence.claim: DeLand’s Woodland Boulevard historic district
evidence.quote: Downtown DeLand's main street, Woodland Boulevard, has a number of notable 19th-century buildings. It is officially known as Downtown DeLand Historic District.

evidence.claim: Farther north, US 17 carries the corridor to the Volusia County line; SR 11 forms another leg, reached from SR 40.
evidence.quote: At US 17, you are on the River of Lakes Heritage Corridor. You can either head north on US 17 to the Volusia County line.

evidence.claim: SR 11 forms another leg, reached from SR 40.
evidence.quote: you can continue on SR 40 past US 17 to SR 11 which is another leg of the corridor.

evidence.claim: In winter, manatees gather at Blue Spring State Park.
evidence.quote: Blue Spring State Park, where manatees gather in winter

evidence.claim: Blue Spring’s 73-degree Fahrenheit water attracts manatees during winter.
evidence.quote: Due to its relatively warm temperature of 73 °F (23 °C), the spring attracts many Florida manatees during the winter.

evidence.claim: It is the largest spring on the St. Johns River, but it was also a transport stop.
evidence.quote: The spring in the park (Volusia Blue Spring) is the largest on the St. Johns River.

evidence.claim: By 1868, Louis Thursby ran a steamboat landing here, and his wife Mary served as postmistress.
evidence.quote: By 1868 Thursby was running a steamboat landing on the river, and Blue Spring became a regular mail stop with his wife Mary as postmistress.

evidence.claim: In 1872, he built a two-story frame house on a shell midden at the mouth of the spring run.
evidence.quote: In 1872 he built a two-story frame house on top of the shell midden at the mouth of the run

evidence.claim: His son later added a third story.
evidence.quote: His son John later added a third story to the house

evidence.claim: The park service restored the house to its 1915 appearance, and the maintained building contains historical displays.
evidence.quote: The park service decided to restore it to its 1915 appearance

evidence.claim: the maintained building contains historical displays.
evidence.quote: The old Thursby plantation house is being maintained and has historical displays that visitors can explore.

evidence.claim: Shell middens line the riverbanks and the spring run.
evidence.quote: Shell middens, line the banks of the St. Johns River and the spring run.

evidence.claim: The Thursby House stands on a shell midden at the mouth of the spring run.
evidence.quote: In 1872 he built a two-story frame house on top of the shell midden at the mouth of the run

evidence.claim: The Thursby House stands on a shell midden at the mouth of the spring run.
evidence.quote: The old Thursby plantation house is being maintained

evidence.claim: The Hatters’ name keeps a hat manufacturer in DeLand’s university story.
evidence.quote: Its various sports teams are called the Hatters.

evidence.claim: Henry Addison DeLand, who made his money in baking soda, established DeLand Academy in 1883.
evidence.quote: Henry Addison DeLand, a baking soda magnate from Fairport, New York

evidence.claim: established DeLand Academy in 1883.
evidence.quote: in 1883, DeLand established DeLand Academy

evidence.claim: DeLand himself never lived in the city throughout the year.
evidence.quote: DeLand never lived in the city year-round

evidence.claim: An 1885 freeze destroyed the orange crop and left his Florida investments nearly worthless.
evidence.quote: his Florida investments were nearly worthless after the freeze

evidence.claim: An 1885 freeze destroyed the orange crop
evidence.quote: in 1885, a freeze destroyed the orange crop.

evidence.claim: He returned north and entrusted the academy to John B. Stetson, his friend and one of its founding trustees.
evidence.quote: DeLand entrusted the academy to his friend, John B. Stetson, a wealthy hat manufacturer from Philadelphia and one of the institution's founding trustees.

evidence.claim: He returned north
evidence.quote: he returned to his home in the North.

evidence.claim: In 1889, the institution became John B. Stetson University.
evidence.quote: In 1889, it was renamed John B. Stetson University in its patron's honor.

evidence.claim: Beyond campus, Woodland Boulevard’s 19th-century buildings form the Downtown DeLand Historic District.
evidence.quote: Downtown DeLand's main street, Woodland Boulevard, has a number of notable 19th-century buildings. It is officially known as Downtown DeLand Historic District.

evidence.claim: The mill beside De Leon Springs is a reconstruction, not the original plantation building.
evidence.quote: For some unknown reason, the mill building was reconstructed in the early 1900s.

evidence.claim: William Williams established Spring Garden plantation in 1804, growing corn, cotton and sugar cane through the labor of enslaved Africans.
evidence.quote: granting land, including the spring, to William Williams in 1804. He established the first plantation, calling it "Spring Garden", where corn, cotton, and sugar cane were grown, using enslaved Africans to perform the work.

evidence.claim: The mill stopped operating in 1864; by the late 1800s, only its wheel remained.
evidence.quote: After the mill stopped operating in 1864, the building deteriorated until only the wheel remained in the late 1800s.

evidence.claim: The building was reconstructed in the early 1900s and renovated in 1961.
evidence.quote: The building again fell into disrepair until it was renovated by the Schwarze family in 1961.

evidence.claim: The spring’s name was also a tourism project: Spring Garden became Ponce de Leon Springs after the railway arrived in 1886.
evidence.quote: The name of the area was changed from Spring Garden to Ponce de Leon Springs to attract tourists after the Jacksonville, Tampa, Key West Railway was constructed in 1886.

evidence.claim: No known records link Ponce de Leon to the spring.
evidence.quote: There are no known records linking Ponce de Leon to the spring.

flags: The official source establishes 156 miles, state designation in 2009 and national designation in 2021, unlike the material’s state-only designation and 99.8 mapped miles. The corridor has multiple legs; the overview describes a south-to-north selection, not a single road covering all 156 miles.
Cache gives little on grades, curves, travel time or the byway campaign. History distinguishes the modern designation from earlier river and rail transport.
Dropped current claim that Blue Spring holds constantly at 73 degrees: cache states a temperature, not year-round constancy. Retained winter attraction to manatees.

Omitted the current claim of continuous pancake-restaurant operation since 1961: a secondary cache page asserts continuity, but no current operator source verifies it. Preserved the park moment and distinguished the reconstructed mill.

The official byway source uses Timucua for its river-name account; Enterprise and De Leon sources specify Mayaca locally and distinguish them from Timucuans. Broad Indigenous summaries omitted because the cache lacks community-authored evidence and has conflicting local descriptions.
No driving-essential closure or permit found for the selected story subjects. Secondary descriptions of seasonal water-access restrictions were not promoted to current visitor guidance.
